items.name: USS Abraham Lincoln to return home after 320 days
items.summary: The USS Abraham Lincoln will return to its homeport in San Diego, California, on Wednesday after 320 days at sea.
items.full_text:
The USS Abraham Lincoln will return to its California homeport after a 320-day deployment that raised concerns over degrading sailor morale and mental health.

The ship left Naval Station San Diego on Nov. 21, 2025, and joined military operations in the Middle East after the U.S. launched the Iran war alongside Israel on Feb. 28.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth will greet sailors when they set foot on American soil for the first time in over 10 months.

“Secretary Hegseth will welcome the USS Lincoln home tomorrow following their deployment,” the Defense Departmentsaid. “Secretary Hegseth will also speak to the crew on the ship, participate in PT and eat lunch with warfighters in the area.”

On Aug. 6, families of loved ones aboard the Lincoln told military officials at a town hall meeting in San Diego, California, that they were concerned about possibilities of self-harm and food shortages.

Military Times reported several days later that two service members attempted to jump overboard, though the circumstances that led to their attempts were unclear.

Acting Navy Secretary Hung Caoconfirmedin a Sept. 22 letter to Congress that eight sailors attempted suicide aboard ships from the USS Abraham Lincoln Carrier Strike Group since the beginning of its deployment.

Sailors and Navy mental health professionalstoldMilitary Times that the psychiatric assistance system meant to help sailors aboard carriers is strained and unable to meet the demands of prolonged combat deployments.

The Lincoln arrived in Thailand on Sept. 2 for its first scheduled port visit in over 260 days.

The ship had previously pulled into Guam on Dec. 11, 2025.

When the Nimitz-class aircraft carrier pulls into port on Wednesday, it will be several days shy of the USS Gerald Ford’s 326-dayrecordfor longest post-Vietnam carrier deployment that it notched earlier in 2026.

Riley Ceder is a Navy reporter at Military Times, where he covers issues directly affecting service members and their families, as well as breaking news.

items.name: USS Dwight D. Eisenhower returns to port after aircraft mishap
items.summary: The USS Dwight D. Eisenhower returned to its homeport in Norfolk, Virginia, after an E/A-18G Growler mishap injured eight service members aboard the ship.
items.full_text:
The Nimitz-class aircraft carrier USS Dwight D. Eisenhower returned home Monday after an aviationaccidentleft eight sailors injured.

The ship pulled into Norfolk, Virginia, a week after naval aviators landing an E/A-18G Growler were forced to eject when the plane’s arresting gear failed.

The cause of the mishap is under investigation.

Search-and-rescue personnel from Helicopter Sea Combat Squadron 7 recovered the aviators from the ocean and returned them to the ship before they were flown off to Naval Medical Center Portsmouth for further medical evaluation.

Six other shipboard personnel were injured during the incident.

One sailor was medically evacuated from the ship to receive further treatment for non-life-threatening injuries at a Norfolk, Virginia, facility.

Another two sailors were flown to Naval Medical Center Portsmouth.

The Navy told Military Times that the E/A-18G Growler that went overboard has not been recovered from the ocean.

The Navy’s investigation will recommend whether the service should salvage the aircraft.

The Eisenhower returned on July 15, 2024, from a nine-month deployment, during which it battled Iran-backed Houthi rebels along the Red Sea.

The ship finished up sea trials in April as part of its planned incremental availability and was conducting carrier qualifications in the Atlantic at the time of the incident.

Riley Ceder is a Navy reporter at Military Times, where he covers issues directly affecting service members and their families, as well as breaking news.
